Single crystals of CoP3 were grown from a stoichiometric melt under a pressure of 3.5 GPa using a wedge-type, cubic-anvil, high-pressure apparatus.
The as-grown boules of CoP3 were cylindrical, about 3.4 mm in diameter, with a number of cracks.
The as-grown CoP3 boules split easily along the radial direction to generate specimens around 1 mm in diameter and 0.3 mm in length.
Powder X-ray diffraction measurements confirmed that the as-grown boules were a single phase of CoP3 with a lattice constant of 7.7067 Å, close to the literature value.
SEM-EDS measurements showed a homogeneous distribution of Co and P atoms in the as-grown boules, with a Co:P ratio of 0.97:3.00, consistent with the stoichiometric composition.
Back-reflection Laue X-ray measurements confirmed that the grown specimens were single crystals, with a (100) crystallographic plane.
The results suggest that CoP3 melts congruently under high pressure, in contrast to its behavior at ambient pressure, where it is believed to be an incongruent melting compound.
The size of the CoP3 single crystals produced in this study is typically around 1 mm in diameter and 0.3 mm in length.
To enlarge the size of the CoP3 single crystals, the authors suggest using a slower cooling rate, applying a more homogeneous pressure, and growing the crystals from a single seed.

The finding that CoP3 melts congruently under high pressure suggests that other skutterudite compounds may also melt congruently under high pressure, which would be advantageous for growing large single crystals.
The authors used a wedge-type, cubic-anvil, high-pressure apparatus to grow the CoP3 single crystals, a technique previously used to enhance the growth of black phosphorus single crystals.
The authors pre-synthesized CoP3 polycrystals by heating the raw materials of Co and P to around 1100°C and sintering for 1 hour under 3.5 GPa pressure.
The as-grown CoP3 boules were characterized by powder X-ray diffraction, SEM-EDS, and back-reflection Laue X-ray measurements.
The temperature in the crucible during crystal growth was estimated by extrapolating a pre-determined temperature calibration curve, as temperatures above 1100°C could not be directly measured.

The authors suggest that the cracks in the as-grown CoP3 boules need to be eliminated to enlarge the size of the single crystals, and that a slower cooling rate or a more homogeneous pressure may help prevent cracking.
